title: Reading Genesis

objectives.can: Read a narrative chapter of Genesis with reduced help.

explanation.summary: Genesis tells its stories with very few words: a chain of narrative verbs, a name or a pronoun to say who acts, and then speech. This lesson reads the first fourteen verses of Genesis 22 with less help than before, and says what to look for as you go.

sections.heading: What you will meet in Genesis
body: Genesis mixes several kinds of text: the opening account of creation, genealogies, short stories, and long family narratives about Abraham, Jacob and Joseph. Its narrative chapters are the easiest long Hebrew prose in the Bible, because the grammar is regular. The same few forms carry the story: the wayyiqtol for the next event, the qatal and the participle for background, and the imperative, the yiqtol and the qatal in speech.

The passage for this lesson is Genesis 22:1–14. The rest of the chapter is 22:15–19, where the messenger of the LORD calls to Abraham a second time and Abraham goes home to Beersheba, and 22:20–24, a list of names. After this lesson you can read them yourself.

sections.heading: Narrative economy
body: A story in Genesis moves by chains of wayyiqtol verbs. The subject is named once and then left understood, and each verb is the next step. In 22:3 the one subject, Abraham, does six things in a row: וַיַּשְׁכֵּם, וַיַּחֲבֹשׁ, וַיִּקַּח, וַיְבַקַּע, וַיָּקָם, וַיֵּלֶךְ. There is no comment on what he thinks or feels. The reader is given actions and has to supply the rest.

Background is given in a different form. A qatal or a participle in a clause that begins with the subject steps outside the chain to tell the reader something. In 22:3 the relative clause אֲשֶׁר אָמַר לוֹ הָאֱלֹהִים has a qatal and says what God had said before Abraham set out. In 22:13 וְהִנֵּה אַיִל … נֶאֱחַז presents the ram, caught, as something Abraham sees. Ask of each clause: is it the next event, or is it background?
Where the story begins with וַיְהִי and a time phrase, as in 22:1, the clause that follows is the setting of the whole scene.

sections.heading: Repetition
body: Genesis repeats on purpose. In 22:6 and again in 22:8 the narrator closes a paragraph with the same words, וַיֵּלְכוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם יַחְדָּו: the two of them go on together. The words are the same, but what lies between them has changed: in between, Isaac has asked his question and Abraham has answered it.

The speakers answer a call with the same short word, הִנֵּנִי, which means roughly 'here I am'. It is הִנֵּה with a suffix. Abraham says it to God in 22:1, to Isaac (as הִנֶּנִּי) in 22:7, and to the messenger of the LORD in 22:11. The verb of taking, וַיִּקַּח, also returns in 22:3, 22:6 and 22:10 each time Abraham makes a new move toward the sacrifice.

In 22:2 the command piles words up before the name: קַח נָא אֶת בִּנְךָ אֶת יְחִידְךָ אֲשֶׁר אָהַבְתָּ אֶת יִצְחָק. Each phrase narrows the object, and the name Isaac is the last word. Read such a sentence to the end before you decide what it means.

sections.heading: Dialogue
body: Speech is introduced by וַיֹּאמֶר and has no quotation marks. A new וַיֹּאמֶר can mean a new speaker or the same speaker beginning again, so ask who is talking each time. In 22:7 there are four in a row: Isaac speaks (אָבִי), Abraham answers (הִנֶּנִּי בְנִי), and Isaac speaks again with his question. The second word of the answer, בְנִי, is a noun with the suffix 'my', and it tells you that a father is speaking to his son.

Speech brings back the forms narrative rarely uses. The imperative gives the commands in 22:2: קַח, לֶךְ, and וְהַעֲלֵהוּ, with the suffix -הוּ for 'him'. The cohortative expresses a resolve of the speaker: נֵלְכָה in 22:5 says 'let us go' or 'we will go' for Abraham and the boy. A prohibition is אַל with a jussive, as in 22:12 אַל תִּשְׁלַח יָדְךָ, 'do not stretch out your hand'. In the same verse the qatal יָדַעְתִּי states knowledge that has now been reached.

sections.heading: Hard places
body: Some places are difficult even though the grammar is plain. In 22:8 Abraham says אֱלֹהִים יִרְאֶה לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה לְעֹלָה. The verb is a form of רָאָה, 'see', with ל; the sense usually given is 'God will see to it', that is, provide, but a hearer in the story may take it more than one way, and the text does not choose for the reader.

In 22:13 the word אַחַר before the ram is the usual reading, 'behind'. Some manuscripts and ancient versions seem to have had a different word at this place, אֶחָד, 'one', and commentators discuss which is likely. A reader works with the text as it stands and keeps in mind that the question exists.

The place-name in 22:14 is explained by a saying with a passive verb, יֵאָמֵר, 'it is said'. The explanation is short, and the verbs in it are the same root as the verb in 22:8, so the name echoes the earlier answer.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read 22:1–14 once for the story. Then read it again and, for each verse, mark whether its verbs are wayyiqtol (the next event), qatal or participle (background), or forms of speech. At each וַיֹּאמֶר, say who speaks. At each suffix, say which earlier word it points back to. Look words up only after you have tried the sentence.

misunderstandings: Reading every wayyiqtol as 'and he did', one after another, without a pause. Some join an action to the one before, and the chain may stop for a speech or for a background clause.
Taking הִנֵּנִי as an announcement of someone's arrival. It is the usual answer to a call and means 'I am here, ready'.
Assuming that a repeated phrase is a copying error. In Genesis repeating is a method of the narrator.
Treating the translation as the Hebrew. English fills in what the Hebrew leaves out, such as what Abraham thinks, and that can hide how little the Hebrew says.

deeper.heading: Narrative and what is left out
body: Readers have long noticed how much Genesis 22 leaves unsaid: no inner thoughts are given, and no reply from Abraham to the command is reported. Scholars explain this in different ways, and the grammar can describe the habit of reporting only actions and speech but cannot decide what the silence means.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son; and he cleaved the wood for the burnt-offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Six wayyiqtol verbs with one subject, Abraham: he rose early, saddled, took, split the wood, set out, and went. Each verb is the next event. Further on the relative clause with the qatal אָמַר steps back to what God had said before.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abraham took the wood of the burnt-offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son; and he took in his hand the fire and the knife; and they went both of them together.

examples.analysis: Two forms of וַיִּקַּח and a וַיָּשֶׂם lead to the closing refrain: וַיֵּלְכוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם יַחְדָּו. The plural verb is followed by שְׁנֵיהֶם, 'the two of them', and the adverb יַחְדָּו, 'together'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Isaac spoke unto Abraham his father, and said: 'My father.' And he said: 'Here am I, my son.' And he said: 'Behold the fire and the wood; but where is the lamb for a burnt-offering?'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A dialogue of four וַיֹּאמֶר in one verse. Isaac speaks, Abraham answers with הִנֶּנִּי, and Isaac asks with הִנֵּה and the question word וְאַיֵּה, 'and where'. The only way to find the speaker is to follow the vocative and the content.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Lay not thy hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him; for now I know that thou art a God-fearing man, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son, from Me.'

examples.analysis: The speech of the messenger of the LORD. אַל with the jussive תִּשְׁלַח, and again with תַּעַשׂ, forms the prohibitions. Then the qatal יָדַעְתִּי says that the knowledge has now been reached, and וְלֹא חָשַׂכְתָּ names the reason: you did not hold back.

examples.analysis: וַיַּרְא leads into וְהִנֵּה, which presents the ram as Abraham sees it. The word אַחַר is the usual reading, and נֶאֱחַז, a Niphal qatal, says that the ram was caught. This is one of the places where some witnesses read another word.

options: They report one action after another, all by Abraham
They give a list of commands to Abraham
They report what the servants did
They describe what Abraham was in the habit of doing
practice.explain: All six are wayyiqtol, the form for the next event in a story. The subject Abraham is named once and understood for the rest.

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place afar off.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Abraham said unto his young men: 'Abide ye here with the ass, and I and the lad will go yonder; and we will worship, and come back to you.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Abraham took the wood of the burnt-offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son; and he took in his hand the fire and the knife; and they went both of them together.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Isaac spoke unto Abraham his father, and said: 'My father.' And he said: 'Here am I, my son.' And he said: 'Behold the fire and the wood; but where is the lamb for a burnt-offering?'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Abraham said: 'God will provide Himself the lamb for a burnt-offering, my son.' So they went both of them together.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And they came to the place which God had told him of; and Abraham built the altar there, and laid the wood in order, and bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar, upon the wood.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Abraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And the angel of the LORD called unto him out of heaven, and said: 'Abraham, Abraham.' And he said: 'Here am I.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And he said: 'Lay not thy hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him; for now I know that thou art a God-fearing man, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son, from Me.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in the thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt-offering in the stead of his son.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Genesis
segments.english: And Abraham called the name of that place Adonai-jireh; as it is said to this day: 'In the mount where the LORD is seen.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

authoring.by: Written for Ecclesia by Claude (Anthropic), following the public-domain grammars listed as sources. Every Hebrew word shown as an example, in a paradigm or in an exercise is taken from the Westminster Leningrad Codex as analysed by the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible project.
